summary: Federal AI use is publicly inventoried; GAO audits it, and the state legislatures writing AI law are tracked on this site.

analysis.body:
The U.S. Government Accountability Office documented that twenty of twenty-three major federal agencies reported approximately 1,200 current and planned AI use cases, while three agencies reported having no uses for AI at all. Most of those reported cases were still in the planning phase rather than in active production, and only in about 200 instances did agencies report that they were currently using AI operationally. Reported applications included analyzing data from cameras and radar to identify border activities, examining photographs from drones, and targeting scientific specimens for planetary rovers. NASA and the Department of Commerce reported the highest number of AI use cases among the agencies surveyed.

Per GAO, the inventory data underlying these figures carries significant reliability problems. Only five of the twenty agencies that reported use cases provided comprehensive information for each one, while the remaining fifteen had instances of incomplete or inaccurate data. Some inventories omitted required elements such as the AI life cycle stage, and two inventories included uses that the agencies themselves later determined were not actually AI. GAO concluded that without accurate inventories, the government's ability to manage its use of AI will be materially hindered.

Compliance with federal AI requirements is uneven. GAO found that ten of twenty-three agencies implemented all AI requirements specific to their agencies, twelve implemented some but not all, and one was exempt. The Office of Management and Budget had not yet developed guidance for the acquisition and use of AI, a gap GAO identified as preventing agencies from consistently managing AI across the government. The Office of Personnel Management had not yet established or updated an occupational category for employees performing AI work, and the Office of Science and Technology Policy had not communicated which agencies were expected to fulfill specific requirements.

On the funding side, GAO noted that the President's fiscal year 2023 budget request included 1.8 billion dollars for nondefense research and development investment in AI. The General Services Administration established an AI Center of Excellence, and the Department of Commerce created a plan to develop AI technical standards, making those two agencies among the further-along implementers by the measures GAO applied.

The international and legislative picture is tracked by several organizations. OECD.AI monitors national AI strategies, public-sector initiatives, and ethical frameworks across member and partner countries, and gives access to more than 900 national AI policies and initiatives. Oxford Insights produces a Government AI Readiness Index that scores countries on policy capacity, governance, infrastructure, and public-sector adoption, offering a standard cross-national comparison. Stanford HAI's annual AI Index carries a government and policy track covering legislation counts, national strategy execution, and public-sector procurement, and the 2026 edition noted a widening gap between what AI can do and how prepared governments are to manage it. On the domestic legislative front, this site tracks 2,428 AI bills across 53 jurisdictions, updated daily, reflecting the pace at which state legislatures are moving to write AI law even as federal guidance remains incomplete.

For any organization considering deployment in or alongside government, the GAO record suggests that the foundational work of simply knowing what AI is in use, where it sits in its life cycle, and whether it meets compliance requirements remains unfinished at most federal agencies. The absence of government-wide acquisition guidance means procurement practices vary, and the density of incoming state legislation tracked across all 50 states adds a layered and rapidly shifting regulatory environment that any vendor or agency deploying AI must monitor continuously.
